https://www.dw.com/en/iran-president-def.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JHZu Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said economic risk must be lifted if the Islamic Republic is to attract foreign investment Image: Iranian Presidential Office/AFP Advertisement Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday defended Tehran's expired Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the United States as the best option for ending hostilities between the two nations, which Pezeshkian described as being "neither war nor peace." Pezeshkian said members of Iran 's Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) agreed with the assessment on the basis of, "dignity, wisdom and national interest." "There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation," Pezeshkian said in remarks published by state-run news agency IRNA. "The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path." The MoU, signed by US President Donald Trump in June, laid out a 60-day timeline for ending the US-Israeli-led conflict as well as ensuring that Iran give up its nuclear ambitions. The deadline passed last week with no signs of compromise by either side, and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz — which Iran closed in response to US-Israeli attacks, putting the global economy in a chokehold for the past six months — still unresolved. On Sunday, Pezeshkian called it imperative that Iran exit this stalled phase of the conflict to unlock foreign investment to the country. "Capital and money are extremely sensitive to risk," he said. "We have to remove this risk from the country." US-Iran war: Will it ever end? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Pakistani mediator expected in Tehran as hardliner warns neighbors not to help US Iran's Foreign Ministry on Sunday announced that Pakistan 's top military leader, Asim Munir, will travel to Iran on Monday. The visit is part of "Pakistan's ongoing efforts to help consolidate peace and security in the region," Tehran said. Pakistan was instrumental in getting the MoU between Washington and Tehran signed. Earlier this month, Islamabad signed its own regional security cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, which observers read as an attempt to counter Iranian influence in the region. Still, despite news of Munir's travels and Pezeshkian's announcement that the SNSC backs the MoU, that body's new hardline leader, Mohsen Rezaei, warned neighboring countries against aiding the US war effort , saying, "If [Trump] wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner." Rezaei said Iran would target oil-shipping routes out of the Persian Gulf — alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz — if neighbors join the US economic war against Iran. Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war? https://www.somersetcountygazette.co.uk/.text: Clarks Village Events Leisure Pets Shopping Street Clarks Village shopping outlet to host dog-friendly weekend By Jack Roberts Reporter Share 0 Comments Clarks Village in Street will host the Pawsome Pooch event on Saturday, September 12, and Sunday, September 13 (Image: Supplied) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A shopping outlet in Street is rolling out the red carpet for dogs with a weekend of tail-wagging fun. Clarks Village will host the Pawsome Pooch event on Saturday, September 12, and Sunday, September 13, offering a packed schedule of free canine-friendly activities, including pampering, trick training, agility sessions and professional pet photo shoots. The event promises to be a highlight for dogs and owners alike, with a ‘dog walk’ giving pups the chance to show off their freshly groomed looks. For the first time, a matchmaking activity for single owners will also be introduced, with dogs donning red bows in the hope of sniffing out a connection. Mike Jones, centre director at Clarks Village, said: "Due to popular demand, we’ve made Pawsome Pooch bigger and better than ever before with a full dog-takeover of Clarks Village for an entire weekend. "Jam-packed with free, tail-wagging activities, it’s our way of celebrating our canine companions and showcasing our dog-friendly facilities and ethos where every member of the family is welcome." Returning to the event are three 'Very Important Pups' - the current Canine Executive Officer (CEO), Archie the golden miniature dachshund; Dudley, the three-legged Hungarian Vizsla and former 'CEO'; and Bailey the whippet, the original Pawsome Pooch winner. The trio will unveil their portraits in a new 'CEO' Hall of Fame at the outlet. The centrepiece of the weekend will be the search for Clarks Village’s next 'CEO', with the winner receiving a prize package worth up to £500. This includes shopping vouchers, dog treats, toys and vouchers for restaurants and retailers at the outlet. The event runs from 11am to 4pm on both days, with all activities free of charge. Guests are encouraged to sign up to the Clarks Village PLUS+ member rewards scheme to book a photo shoot. https://www.politico.eu/article/franco-g.text: BRUSSELS — France and Germany on Thursday failed to agree a common position on the scope of the bloc’s future “Made in Europe” rules, as well as on greater flexibility for CO2 emissions cuts and the 2035 combustion engine ban. The draft quid-pro-quo deal, which was first reported by POLITICO in July , marks a major convergence between the two countries and had been expected to be signed imminently. On Thursday evening, however, the agreement stalled amid opposition from Germany’s Social Democratic Party, the center-left junior partner in the ruling coalition, over concerns it dropped key environmental targets. “A final agreement has yet to be reached,” a German government spokesperson said. Advertisement Advertisement Earlier this week, French President Emmanuel Macron had suggested the ball was in the German court. “There are political constraints on the other side of the Rhine, and I completely respect coalition discussions,” Macron said Monday on the sidelines of the Paris car show. Under the terms of the proposed deal, Germany would accept stricter Made in Europe criteria for the automotive sector in the Industrial Accelerator Act, which France has pushed for, in exchange for weakening the combustion engine ban, one of Berlin’s long-term demands. "In light of the significant technological, economic and geopolitical changes since the existing regulatory framework was established, the Automotive Package should strike a better balance between climate objectives, industrial competitiveness, technological development and the strengthening of European value creation," the two countries wrote in a draft agreement obtained by POLITICO . "Based on the Franco-German Ministerial Councils in 2025 and 2026, Germany and France therefore propose a balanced negotiating package combining ambitious CO₂ reduction targets with additional flexibility and targeted incentives for European value creation," the agreement adds. Currently, the EU's target is for companies to reduce combustion engine emissions by 100% from 2021 levels by 2035, with the possibility to 'earn' 10% of emissions leeway through initiatives like offsets and investments. Under the proposed deal, France and Germany want to soften the 2035 target to 90%, and to offer a further 10% leeway in exchange for investments in alternative fuels (for a combined 80%). Advertisement Advertisement Crucially for steel manufacturers and Germany’s leftist SPD, the French-German agreement would axe the green steel investment requirement, removing a key incentive. “This destroys the lead market for the steel industry,” an industry lobbyist told POLITICO on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive topic. In failing to put pressure on automakers to source green steel, the draft deal makes it a “nice-to-have” extra, they explained. In a concession to Berlin, the draft agreement stresses that the so-called utility factor — which calculates plug-in hybrid emissions based on how often a vehicle’s electric motor is used vs. its combustion engine — should be calculated on lab-based results rather than real-world data, as required by the Commission. The change will help automakers sell more plug-in hybrids while still reaching the broader emissions targets. In exchange for these emissions concessions, Germany endorsed France’s demand that the scope of the Made in Europe rules under the bloc’s Industrial Accelerator Act be restricted when it comes to the automotive sector. The text only covers the EU’s 27 member countries and will be extended to the U.K. under certain conditions. EU industry chief Stéphane Séjourné told POLITICO on Tuesday that he supported the deal as a way of breaking the impasse, and said the U.K. currently qualifies for Made in Europe. Advertisement Advertisement The agreement could resolve a stalemate over both the CO2 regulation and the IAA, in which France and Germany have been on opposite sides. “The elements of this combined package should be adopted as soon as possible and at the same time,” the two countries wrote. The British government welcomed the potential inclusion of the U.K. in the Made in Europe rules for cars. “This is a Franco-German proposal and there is still a European process to run, but if confirmed, we welcome the objective to have the U.K. included in the Industrial Accelerator Act, and this would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the U.K.,” a No. 10 official said in a statement. If approved, the comprehensive Franco-German deal will still have to be approved by other EU countries and by the European Parliament, which are currently discussing the Industrial Accelerator Act and the automotive package, including emissions targets for automakers. Carlo Martuscelli, Francesca Micheletti and Graham Lanktree contributed to this report.

https://www.breitbart.com/politics/2026/.text: RIGA, Latvia (AP) – Latvians are electing a new parliament on Saturday as pro-Ukraine Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs seeks a full term. The vote comes as the small republic on NATO’s eastern flank contends with growing concern about potential Russian aggression. A political crisis in May over the handling of stray drones suspected to be from Ukraine brought down the governing coalition that had been under strain due to multiple other issues. The parliament, or Saeima, then approved a four-party coalition led by Kulbergs of the centrist United List party, previously in opposition. Latvia, like its Baltic neighbors Lithuania and Estonia, strongly supports Ukraine in its fight against Moscow’s invasion. It borders both Russia and Moscow-allied Belarus. Kulbergs, 47, is now seeking his own mandate from voters. “I hope we get a good result. This would give us an opportunity to make changes, put Latvia on the right track for defense and economy,” he said outside a polling station in Riga after casting his ballot. “A strong economy can only bring strong defense, so that is the mission for the next four years if I´m given the right to lead the country,” he added. “Our party is ready to make changes.” A multiparty coalition will almost certainly be needed to govern in a splintered political landscape. Parties must take at least 5% of the vote to win parliamentary seats. “What I want to see is just democracy in action, just people actually going to vote and voicing their opinions on who they want to govern the country for the next term,” said Janis Artis Briedis, who voted in Riga. Nearly 1.56 million people in the nation of more than 1.8 million are entitled to choose the 100 members of the single-chamber Saeima for a four-year term. “It’s obviously a very decisive election, and I expect that we’ll vote for parties that will be making nationally correct decisions for the defense and the economy, so I think the coalition will be maybe not ideal, but it will be still OK and we’ll be moving in the right direction,” Reinholds Pirags said after voting. Concern about potential Russian hybrid attacks – a term used for non-conventional hostile acts such as sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and an array of other methods – has been mounting across parts of Europe in recent months; Latvia, among other nations on NATO´s eastern edge, is particularly exposed. NATO has reinforced its protection of Latvian airspace for the election period, with Germany sending four Eurofighter jets to Latvia for about a week. The Latvian State Security Service said last week that it hadn’t yet detected any significant or systematic efforts by Russia or others to influence the election in favor of any party or candidate, the LETA news agency reported. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwj3.text: Image source, Villa Vie Residences Image caption, The Villa Vie Odyssey was more than 750 days into its voyage around the world when it came to a stop in Cambodia By Koh Ewe Â and Â Claire Graham ,Â BBC News NI Published 28 October 2026, 03:05 GMT Updated 1 hour ago A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia. The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements". It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world". Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (Â£6,000) from $1,800. Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs". "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said. The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said. There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres. The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website. Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds. The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia. Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day. The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out. "Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed." "There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened." Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed". Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said. "It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia. "We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting." Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport. Image source, Supplied Image caption, Cruise passenger Holly Hennessey and her cat, Captain, have now found themselves in Cambodia During their time onboard the Villa Vie Odyssey, passengers had access to several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website. Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month. Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea. In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package. Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election". For Canen and Bodin the experience was "worth it", despite the fact it was shorter than expected. "We loved our two years on Odysseyâthe adventures, the places we visited and the friends we made along the way." Many of the passengers have already made plans to "settle together off the ship, so those friendships and that sense of community are continuing on land", they said. The couple plans to spend a few days in Sihanoukville, before travelling to different parts of South East Asia while they "figure out our next chapter". But others, like Hennessey, have decided to stick around in Cambodia in the hopes that the Odyssey will set sail again soon. "Until they say we are done - done done - I am not giving up. I could never duplicate this lifestyle. The idea of going home? It would be so trite," she said. "Cambodia's not the worst place to hang out." Additional reporting by Thanya Doksone.
